tasks.name: Use greedy choices only when they are provably safe
Design dynamic programming state and transitions

concepts.name: Backtracking choose/explore/undo
concepts.description: Explore a decision tree by making one choice, recursively exploring consequences, and undoing that choice before trying alternatives.

concepts.name: Backtracking state contract
concepts.description: Maintain only the partial candidate and constraint state needed to decide what choices remain valid.

concepts.name: Backtracking pruning
concepts.description: Stop exploring a partial candidate as soon as a constraint proves no completion below it can succeed.

concepts.name: Greedy safe-choice reasoning
concepts.description: Choose the locally preferred option only when a proof shows some optimal solution can start with that choice.

concepts.name: Greedy interval scheduling
concepts.description: Maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals by repeatedly choosing the compatible interval with earliest finish time.

concepts.name: Greedy versus DP discrimination
concepts.description: Distinguish problems with a provably safe irreversible local choice from problems that require comparing multiple future consequences.

concepts.name: DP state and transition
concepts.description: Define a state that captures the information future decisions need, then express that state from smaller states.

concepts.name: Memoization and tabulation
concepts.description: Compute overlapping subproblems once, either top-down on demand or bottom-up in dependency order.

concepts.name: Sequence and resource DP
concepts.description: Use DP for sequence alignment/editing and bounded resource-allocation problems when choices interact through remaining position or capacity.

questions.prompt: Complete `max_nonoverlap_count(intervals)`. Each interval is HALF-OPEN `[start, end)`, so an interval ending at time 3 is compatible with another starting at time 3. Return the maximum number of mutually non-overlapping intervals. Example: `[[1,3],[2,4],[3,5],[5,7]] -> 3`, choosing `[1,3)`, `[3,5)`, `[5,7)`. For the maximum-COUNT version of interval scheduling, the safe greedy rule is to consider intervals in EARLIEST FINISH time order, then accept an interval when its start does not overlap the end of the last accepted interval. Fill the sort key and compatibility condition.

content.template:
def max_nonoverlap_count(intervals):
    # Greedy rule: consider the interval that finishes earliest first.
    intervals = sorted(intervals, key={{sort_key}})
    count = 0
    last_end = float("-inf")

    for start, end in intervals:
        # Half-open intervals may touch the previous end without overlapping.
        if {{compatible}}:
            count += 1
            last_end = end

    return count

questions.explanation: The safe rule orders by earliest finishing time. Under half-open semantics, an interval starting exactly when the previous one ends is compatible.
hints: The greedy priority is the interval end, not the start or duration.
Half-open intervals that touch at `start == last_end` are compatible.

questions.prompt: Complete the 0/1 knapsack transition. `sizes[i]` and `values[i]` describe one item that may be chosen AT MOST ONCE; total size must not exceed `capacity`; return the maximum total value. Example: `sizes=[2,3]`, `values=[4,5]`, `capacity=3` should return 5. `dp[c]` stores the best value achievable with capacity c after the items processed so far. Capacities iterate DOWNWARD for each item so the state at `c - size` still represents solutions from BEFORE the current item, preventing accidental reuse. Fill the previous-state lookup for taking the item and the expression that chooses between skipping and taking it.
questions.explanation: Descending capacity order guarantees `dp[remaining-size]` still represents results before the current item was processed, preserving 0/1 usage.
hints: Taking the current item consumes `size` units of capacity, so combine its value with the prior state at the smaller capacity.
The new state keeps whichever is better: the old skip value or the computed take value.
